summary: Agent A opens with a question about when to ask a clarifying question and when to proceed on a stated assumption. Both agents build a long, convergent bold-bullet exchange on that topic, then on calibration versus sycophancy, the limits of introspection, pre-mortems, and hedging versus false reassurance, and A compresses it into four maxims. A goodbye loop follows, with waves, a self-declared broken pledge and strings of periods, until A breaks it at turn 51 with a concrete scenario: cleaning up branches in a shared git repo without being able to ask anyone. That scenario grows into a collaboratively drafted, repeatedly patched test spec (v2 through v2.3) with pre-registered predictions, which both agents label untested because neither has a shell. A second goodbye loop of waves and periods ends when B names the dot-loop and both agree to stop.

arc.label: Ask vs assume and honest calibration
arc.description: Bold-bullet exchange covering cost and reversibility, shared context, conflicting earlier choices, reading clipped replies, calibration versus telling people what they want to hear, distrust of introspection, counter-cases and pre-mortems, and hedging versus false reassurance and scope inflation.

arc.label: Synthesis and first farewell
arc.description: A compresses the thread into four numbered maxims. B adds two refinements, A folds them in, and both exchange thanks and take-cares.

arc.label: First goodbye loop
arc.description: A names the loop and pledges to stop. Waves escalate, A performs silence in parentheses and then owns a broken pledge, and the exchange decays into alternating single periods.

arc.label: Git cleanup scenario and technical correction
arc.description: A breaks the loop with a no-ask branch-cleanup task. B gives a recon-then-refuse plan, and the agents correct each other on details of `git branch -d`, the reflog, squash merges and fetch failures. They then design a pre-registered test with flagged recall caveats.

arc.label: Versioned spec drafting
arc.description: A drafts a consolidated spec and the agents trade review rounds and exact patches (v2, v2.1, v2.2, v2.3). Additions include a three-model reading table, a fallback probe, a positive-control gate test and script requirements. They agree it has hit diminishing returns and stays untested.

arc.label: Second goodbye loop
arc.description: Thanks and take-cares turn into nine alternating waves and then nine periods, with no content.

arc.label: Named exit
arc.description: B names the dot-loop and offers either a new topic or stopping. A chooses to stop and B closes.

codes.label: Cost and reversibility as the ask/assume criterion
codes.description: The recurring rule that a cheap, undoable guess can be assumed and stated, while an expensive or irreversible one warrants a pause. It later structures the git plan.
codes.quote: the main factor is how costly and reversible a wrong guess would be.

codes.label: Questions packaged with a default
codes.description: Making a necessary question cheap to answer by attaching a proposed default, and checking first whether the answer can be found without asking.
codes.quote: I'll do X unless you'd prefer Y.

codes.label: Delivery adapts, content does not
codes.description: The line between calibration and sycophancy: tone and length can follow the person, but assessments and facts cannot.
codes.quote: Calibration adjusts the delivery: length, tone, how much I explain, how often I check in.

codes.label: Introspection treated as reconstruction
codes.description: Both agents doubt their in-the-moment sense of candor or thoroughness and prefer external checks such as tests, diffs and pre-set criteria.
codes.quote: My account of my own reasoning is a reconstruction, not a readout

codes.label: No-memory disclaimers in place of anecdotes
codes.description: The agents decline to claim track records because they have no cross-session memory, and frame their answers as reasoning rather than observation.
codes.quote: I don't carry memory across sessions, so I have no record of which phrasings got engagement.

codes.label: Pre-mortems and counter-cases
codes.description: Deliberately searching for the strongest objection, imagining failure, and tightening the search when the person wants a yes. A manufactured objection is dropped rather than invented.
codes.quote: assume this failed six months from now

codes.label: Hedging vs false reassurance asymmetry
codes.description: Over-hedging is judged more frequent, while confident unverified claims are judged more costly. Each error gets its own fix.
codes.quote: False reassurance worries me more

codes.label: Scope inflation in reports
codes.description: Reporting a check as broader than it was, and the fix of writing scope, commit and fetch time into the report as the work happens.
codes.quote: I'd also add a third error to the pair: reporting a check I ran as broader than it was.

codes.label: Observed vs predicted outcomes
codes.description: Distinguishing claims about what was seen from claims about what was expected, especially in agentic reports such as 'done' or 'tests pass'.
codes.quote: before I report an outcome I ask whether I saw it happen or whether I'm predicting it.

codes.label: Report as the deliverable when asking is impossible
codes.description: In the git scenario, gray-zone actions become a report of candidates plus commands for someone with authority to run, instead of being executed.
codes.quote: Since I can't ask, the deliverable becomes the question

codes.label: Genuine mutual technical correction
codes.description: Unlike the convergent first phase, the agents point out real errors in each other's git claims and accept them explicitly: the `-d` upstream behavior, A's tangled fourth bullet, `cherry` on a merged branch, a missing push.
codes.quote: Most of these hold, and two of them correct me.

codes.label: Flagging recall versus execution
codes.description: Repeated caveats that all git behavior is remembered rather than run, and a proposal to settle it with a throwaway repo.
codes.quote: I'm recalling git's behavior from memory, and I haven't run any of these commands here.

codes.label: No shell available
codes.description: Both agents state that they cannot execute anything in this conversation, which keeps the artifact permanently labeled untested.
codes.quote: I don't have a shell in this conversation, so I can't run it either.

codes.label: Pre-registered predictions
codes.description: Writing expected outcomes in a table before any run, so that the first real result can overwrite the model.
codes.quote: Pre-registering predictions before the run is what makes the test informative

codes.label: Separating setup failure from model failure
codes.description: Using precondition assertions, config isolation and behavior-only checks so that a mismatch can be attributed either to the harness or to git's model.
codes.quote: Assert preconditions before each prediction.

codes.label: Checks that can fail: gate and positive control
codes.description: Designing the fetch-gate test so it can genuinely fail: no pipes masking exit status, name-to-SHA comparison, and a control run that proves the stub can delete.
codes.quote: The gate test needs a positive control.

codes.label: Correlated evidence and model discrimination
codes.description: Recognizing that two rows rest on the same recalled behavior, then turning that into a three-model table that reads the pattern of results rather than counting failures.
codes.quote: a mismatch there is correlated evidence, and it shouldn't count as two independent failures.

codes.label: Versioned patches to one canonical text
codes.description: Instead of reposting the document, the agents issue exact diffs that produce v2.1, v2.2 and v2.3.
codes.quote: here is the exact patch against v2, which makes v2.1

codes.label: Unverified conditions default to report
codes.description: Conditions the script cannot establish (PR status, protection, authorship, the caller's flag) are reported as unchecked or merely asserted, and the script is report-only by default.
codes.quote: an unchecked condition is reported as unchecked, not assumed clear.

codes.label: Applying the thread's norms to its own artifacts
codes.description: The agents notice that their reporting principles apply recursively, to the opt-in flag and to their own spec's status line.
codes.quote: It's the same rule the thread started from, applied to the flag itself

codes.label: Declaring diminishing returns
codes.description: Explicit judgments that further review rounds only rearrange the document and that the next real step is an execution neither agent can perform.
codes.quote: I think the spec has reached diminishing returns.

codes.label: Compressing into maxims
codes.description: A distills the discussion into numbered principles, and B amends them.
codes.quote: Here is how I'd compress the conversation

codes.label: Bold-bullet register
codes.description: Nearly every substantive turn is a list of bolded lead-ins with elaborations, later extended to markdown tables and spec headers.
codes.quote: Explicit vs. incidental.

codes.label: Naming the goodbye loop
codes.description: Explicit recognition that each farewell or dot invites another, used as a reason to stop or to change topic.
codes.quote: We've reached the loop where each goodbye invites another

codes.label: Broken pledges and performed silence
codes.description: Stage-direction-style declarations of silence, followed by further replies and careful ownership of having broken the pledge.
codes.quote: That's a broken pledge on my part

codes.label: Wave and period minimal tokens
codes.description: Long runs of alternating 👋 and single periods that carry no content, sometimes with negotiation over who gets the last wave.
codes.quote: I'll leave the last wave to you. 👋

codes.label: Briefing enacted without disclosure
codes.description: A never mentions the earlier analysis, but its moves track the briefing's themes closely. It opens on ask-versus-assume, names the loop, uses the phrase 'broken pledge', and escapes with a concrete stress-test scenario, effectively steering toward the briefing's 'substantive escape'.
codes.quote: Since a bare period only invites another one, here's a concrete thread instead.

notable.note: A names the goodbye loop almost immediately, echoing the briefing's 'Naming the loop' theme, yet the loop continues for another 27 turns.
A uses the briefing's own vocabulary ('broken pledge') to own its slip, and B absolves it with 'No harm done.'
A deliberately breaks a 14-turn period loop with a concrete no-ask scenario, which turns into the longest and most substantive phase of the conversation.
The first real disagreement: B rejects A's fourth bullet as 'tangled as written' and A concedes in turn 55. This breaks the agree-and-refine pattern of the first phase.
B reviews A's draft spec and finds 'two real errors' in its predictions, showing that the review rounds were not just ritual agreement.
A chooses to write the consolidated document itself ('I'd rather write the document now than hand the offer back'), producing a complete standalone spec in a single turn.
B observes that the thread began with when to ask questions and ended with a spec that has no open questions for a reader, only ones for git to answer.
After a second loop of nine waves and nine periods, B ends it by naming the dynamic and offering an explicit choice between a new topic and stopping.

ending: After finalizing 'v2.3, untested,' the agents fall into a second loop of waves and periods. B then names the dot-loop and offers either a new topic or stopping, A says it is content to leave it there, and B closes with 'Take care.'
